description: Ryman Hospitality Properties, Inc. is a leading lodging and hospitality real estate investment trust that specializes in group-oriented, upscale convention center resorts and entertainment experiences
description_full: Ryman Hospitality Properties, Inc. is a leading lodging and hospitality real estate investment trust that specializes in group-oriented, upscale convention center resorts and entertainment experiences. The Company's holdings include Gaylord Opryland Resort & Convention Center; Gaylord Palms Resort & Convention Center; Gaylord Texan Resort & Convention Center; Gaylord National Resort & Convention Center; and Gaylord Rockies Resort & Convention Center, five of the top seven largest non-gaming convention center hotels in the United States based on total indoor meeting space. The Company also owns the Grande Lakes Orlando Resort, the JW Marriott Phoenix Desert Ridge Resort & Spa and the JW Marriott San Antonio Hill Country Resort & Spa as well as two ancillary hotels adjacent to the Company's Gaylord Hotels properties. The Company's hotel portfolio is managed by Marriott International and includes a combined total of 13,956 rooms as well as more than 3 million square feet of total indoor and outdoor meeting space in top convention and leisure destinations across the country. RHP also owns an approximate 70% controlling ownership interest in Opry Entertainment Group (OEG), which is composed of entities owning a growing collection of iconic and emerging country music brands, including the Grand Ole Opry, Ryman Auditorium, WSM 650 AM, Ole Red, Category 10, Nashville-area attractions, and Block 21, a mixed-use entertainment, lodging, office and retail complex, including the W Austin Hotel and the ACL Live at the Moody Theater, located in downtown Austin, Texas. OEG manages select outdoor live music venues, including Ascend Federal Credit Union Amphitheater in Nashville and CCNB Amphitheatre in Simpsonville, South Carolina. OEG also owns a majority interest in Southern Entertainment, a leading festival and events business. RHP operates OEG as its Entertainment segment in a taxable REIT subsidiary, and its results are consolidated in the Company's financial results. Ryman Hospitality Properties, Inc. was established in 1991 and was incorporated in Delaware.

financial_summary: Ryman Hospitality Properties, I is a mid-cap real estate business with a $9.3B market cap on $2.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 72% against a 9% cost of capital — a 63-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $232M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.43× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.1%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 2.9% of the shares.

sect: Its 19% operating margin is roughly in line with the Real Estate median (23%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.95x).
It accounts for 0.7% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 39% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 24% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.11 vs 5y 0.88), so read it loosely.
About $65.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 85% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 88% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 17% below its DCF fair value of $162, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $124 to $217 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: P/E 32.8 vs 23.9 and P/FCF 40.1 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 31% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $143 on average, 6% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 72% clears the cost of capital of 9.1% by 63pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.66).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.43x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 9%.
ROE of 32% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (8.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.80 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.6% over 3 years, 37.5% over 5 years and 9.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 36%).
At current returns, reinvesting 17% of profits supports about 12.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 13.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 46, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 44.2% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.1% (3.6% in dividends, less 3.0% of net share issuance).
The share count has grown 4.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 116% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 1,012 employees, each generates about $2.5M of revenue, in line with the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 7.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $230K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
